cards.text: In 2024 Japan picked three projects planning to store about 10 million tonnes of CO2 a year off Malaysia. No tonne has shipped, and no Japan–Malaysia agreement is signed.
cards.sub: Two sites lie off Peninsular Malaysia, under the 2025 federal CCUS Act. Sarawak regulates the third under its own 2023 ordinance.
sources: METI/JOGMEC, Advanced CCS Projects selection, 28 Jun 2024 (planned capacities): Northern Offshore Peninsular (~3 Mtpa), Offshore Sarawak (~1.9-2.9 Mtpa), Southern Offshore Peninsular (~5 Mtpa, 'offshore of the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia') [brief S7]; JOGMEC FY2025 stage-gate status unverified
Petronas, 1 Apr 2026: no agreement signed with Japan; bilateral agreement needed (reported) [S15]; Ministry of Economy, 15 Sep 2026: meetings 'towards the finalisation of bilateral agreements' [S9a]

Act 870 s. 2 ('This Act shall apply to Peninsular Malaysia and the Federal Territory of Labuan') [S1a p. 8]; Sarawak Environment (Reduction of Greenhouse Gases Emission) Ordinance 2023, s. 3 and First Schedule [S8]

cards.h: On 23 Oct 2026 Petronas, TotalEnergies and Mitsui signed a joint venture for a CO2 storage hub off Peninsular Malaysia's east coast: up to 5 million tonnes a year, first injection as early as 2031.
cards.s: The hub is built to take Malaysian and regional CO2, including cross-border shipments. It is one of three Malaysian sites on Japan's 2024 list; its investment decision is pending.
cards.d: Southern CCS Hub joint venture agreement signed 23 Oct 2026 by Petronas CCS Ventures, TotalEnergies and Mitsui: 'expected injection capacity of up to 5 million tonnes per annum' in phase 1, first injection 'as early as 2031', final investment decision 'in the near future'. The hub 'is being developed to receive CO2 domestically and regionally, including potential cross-border CO2 shipments', so its 5 Mtpa is hub capacity, not Japanese tonnes. METI's 2024 list names no Petronas company for the Southern project ('closely working with Petronas and TotalEnergies'); Petronas CCS Ventures later signed the JV. JOGMEC selected nine Advanced CCS Projects on 28 Jun 2024 that 'aim to store approximately 20 Mtpa of CO2 in total', five in Japan and four in the Asia-Pacific; three store off Malaysia (Northern Offshore Peninsular about 3 Mtpa, evaluated as 'promising but further initial studies were required'; Offshore Sarawak about 1.9 to 2.9 Mtpa; Southern Offshore Peninsular about 5 Mtpa). Sum about 9.9 to 10.9 Mtpa (FORA arithmetic), planned capacities, not contracts. Japan's own 2030 goal is 6 to 12 Mtpa of storage. AP's 'by 2030 ... 20 million tons' conflates the two and is not used. Kasawari CCS (3.3 Mtpa, first injection target 2027) stores domestic CO2 and is not part of the Japanese projects.
sources: METI/JOGMEC Advanced CCS Projects list, 28 Jun 2024 [S7]

cards.h: Malaysia's 2025 CCUS Act names the Government as payer of a closed offshore site's long-term care, from a fund whose levy may not be raised when the fund is drawn down.
cards.s: In March 2025 then economy minister Rafizi Ramli was reported as saying the government 'will not bear any costs' of CCUS projects. The levy still has no gazetted rate.
cards.d: Act 870 s. 32(1): once a storage site is closed, 'the obligations relating to monitoring, corrective measures and remediation measures shall be transferred to the Government'; s. 32(2): only after 'a prescribed period has lapsed from the issuance of the closure certificate' and prescribed conditions are met; s. 32(3): the operator keeps 'criminal, contractual or civil law liability ... attributable to the fault, negligence or deceit of the offshore operator'. s. 41(2): the Post-Closure Stewardship Fund holds Government sums, the injection levy ('financial support to the Government') and investment income. s. 42(1): the Fund pays 'costs to be borne by the Government for long-term stewardship of offshore storage sites after the transfer of obligations'; the Act does not cap the Government's exposure at the Fund balance. s. 30(2)(b): the levy 'shall not be increased due to withdrawals from the Fund or risks associated with other offshore storage projects'; s. 30(3)(a): the Agency 'may review' rates every five years. AGC lists to 18 Nov 2026 show no levy order and no import regulations (draft in June 2026); only P.U.(A) 346/2025 (in force 1 Oct 2025). Two law-firm summaries (LH-AG; Skrine, citing Regulation 42(c)) report a minimum of 10 years after the closure certificate before transfer, extendable; the regulation text was not opened. Eco-Business (10 Mar 2025) reported: 'in Malaysia, the government will not bear any costs of CCUS projects, said Rafizi' (reporter's paraphrase) and quoted him that the site contract runs '20 to 30 years – after which [responsibility for the site] will be returned to the government'. The Act applies to Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan (s. 2).
sources: Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage Act 2025 (Act 870): ss. 2, 30, 32, 41, 42 [S1a pp. 8, 23-24, 27-28]
AGC Laws of Malaysia lists for Act 870, checked 18 Nov 2026 [S2]; Ministry of Economy workshop on draft import regulations, 22 Jun 2026 [S9b]
Eco-Business, 10 Mar 2025 (Rafizi, reported) [S20c]; LH-AG 16 Oct 2025 [S10a]; Skrine 10 Oct 2025 (Regulation 42 summary, verification item 13)

cards.h: Under UN climate-reporting guidance, the country that captures CO2 reports it as captured and exported. The country storing it reports any that escapes from the site.
cards.s: The UN climate panel put retention at very likely over 99% across 100 years for well-chosen sites. It also said long-term liability for leaks is 'generally unresolved'.
cards.d: 2006 IPCC Guidelines Vol 2 Ch 5 (p. 5.20): where CO2 is captured in Country A and stored in Country B, 'Country A should report the amount of CO2 captured, any emissions from transport and/or temporary storage that takes place in Country A, and the amount of CO2 exported to Country B. Country B should report the amount of CO2 imported, any emissions from transport and/or temporary storage ... and any emissions from injection and geological storage sites.' Ch 2: captured CO2 is subtracted at source and later emissions from transport, injection and the reservoir 'should be counted in national total emissions'. The 2019 Refinement made no change to Chapter 5. These are inventory-reporting rules, not liability rules; they create no credit, and how Japan's own inventory treats exported CO2 is not confirmed in any source opened. If CO2 injected in one country leaks in another, 'Country A is responsible for reporting the emissions from the geological storage site'. IPCC Special Report on CCS (2005) SPM: the fraction retained in appropriately selected and managed geological reservoirs is 'very likely to exceed 99% over 100 years and is likely to exceed 99% over 1,000 years' (para 25); 'Long-term liability issues associated with the leakage of CO2 to the atmosphere and local environmental impacts are generally unresolved' (para 29); export to a non-party needs an agreement covering 'confirmation and allocation of permitting responsibilities'; it need not allocate long-term liability. The Ministry of Economy's '<0.001%' leakage figure attributed to the IPCC was not found in the IPCC text and is not used. Japan accepted the London Protocol's 2009 export amendment on 16 Dec 2025; Malaysia is not a party; export to a non-party needs an agreement with provisions 'at a minimum equivalent' to the Protocol.
sources: 2006 IPCC Guidelines, Vol 2 Ch 5 s. 5.10 p. 5.20 [S3a]; Ch 2 s. 2.3.4 pp. 2.36-2.37 [S3b]; 2019 Refinement Ch 5 'No Refinement' [S3c]
IPCC Special Report on Carbon Dioxide Capture and Storage (2005), SPM paras 25, 29, pp. 14-15 [S4]
IMO status of treaties, 30 Oct 2026, pp. 399-404 [S5]; LP.3(4) amended Art. 6 [S6a]

cards.text: Carbon storage is sold as a climate service. Under Malaysia's federal law, its last chapter is a public bill: a sealed reservoir the Government pays to watch.
It is like agreeing to take back a sealed storeroom for good once the tenant moves out, before anyone has set the fee that pays for its upkeep.
sources: Act 870 s. 32 transfer; s. 30 levy with no gazetted order [S1a, S2]

cards.text: Malaysia's law already puts the long-term care of a closed site on the Government. Publish the levy rate and the Japan agreement before the first tanker sails, not once they are a fait accompli.
sources: Act 870 ss. 32, 42(1) [S1a]; no levy order gazetted [S2]; bilateral agreement 'towards finalisation', unpublished [S9a]; nothing shipped [S15]

headline_suggestion: Japan plans CO2 storage off Malaysia; Malaysian law leaves closed sites' upkeep to the Government
context_suggestion: Malaysia's CCUS Act 2025 lets CO2 captured abroad be imported for permanent storage. Japan's 2024 list plans three storage sites off Malaysia; the bilateral agreement export requires is still being negotiated.
sources: Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage Act 2025 (Act 870); AGC Laws of Malaysia subsidiary legislation lists (Act 870); 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories Vol 2 Ch 2 and Ch 5; 2019 Refinement; IPCC Special Report on CCS (2005) SPM; IMO Status of Treaties (30 Oct 2026); London Protocol Resolution LP.3(4) and LP.5(14); METI/JOGMEC Advanced CCS Projects (28 Jun 2024); Sarawak Environment (Reduction of Greenhouse Gases Emission) Ordinance 2023; Ministry of Economy / MyCCUS releases (2025-2026); Petronas releases (Oct 2023, Feb 2024, Oct 2025, Oct 2026); Petronas GHG data; LH-AG and Pinsent Masons notes; AP (Feb 2026); Climate Home (Mar 2025); The Star and FMT (Mar 2025)
confidence: Medium-High. HIGH on Act 870 text, AGC lists, IMO treaty status, IPCC Guidelines wording and the METI project list. MEDIUM on the post-closure period: the Act says 'a prescribed period'; the 'at least 10 years' figure comes from a law-firm summary of P.U.(A) 346/2025, whose text was not opened. MEDIUM on the Sarawak side: the 2023 Ordinance was opened, the Land (Carbon Storage) Rules 2022 were not. Planned capacities are feasibility-stage, not contracted.
needs_verification: P.U.(A) 346/2025 text: Regulation 42(c) minimum of 10 years before transfer (two law-firm summaries; text not opened). Off the card text; in fact 2's detail only.
No injection-levy order and no import regulations gazetted under Act 870 as at publication (AGC lists checked 18 Nov 2026). Fact 2 sub and the view depend on it.

Rafizi's 'the government will not bear any costs of CCUS projects' is a reporter's paraphrase (Eco-Business, 10 Mar 2025); card attributes it as reported. Check for a primary (Hansard, ministry statement) or keep 'was reported as saying'.
Japan-Malaysia bilateral arrangement status after 15 Sep 2026 ('towards finalisation'); MOFA Joint Statement of 10 Jun 2026 unopened. Hook says 'no Japan–Malaysia agreement is signed'.
JOGMEC FY2025 stage-gate status of the three Malaysian projects; hook dates the list to 2024.
Sarawak Cap. 85 commencement (reported 1 Mar 2024) and the Land (Carbon Storage) Rules 2022; hook sub says only that Sarawak regulates the site under its own ordinance.
source_notes: (1) Post-closure period: Act 870 says 'a prescribed period'; Pinsent Masons (on the Bill, Mar 2025) 'does not specify the duration'; LH-AG (on the Regulations, Oct 2025) 'at least 10 years'; the Economy Minister (Eco-Business paraphrase) '20 to 30 year contract'; NGOs asked for 200 years. Regulation text not opened, so the card avoids a number. (2) 'Liability' vs 'obligations': s. 32 transfers monitoring, corrective and remediation obligations and expressly excludes fault-based liability; cards use 'duties'. (3) AP's '20 million tons by 2030' conflates the nine projects' ~20 Mtpa with Japan's 2030 goal of 6-12 Mtpa; METI used. (4) Kasawari's '1% of Petronas emissions' holds only with Scope 3 included; ~6% of Scope 1+2; off cards, and Kasawari is domestic CO2. (5) Commencement: AGC gives 1 Oct 2025 (P.U.(B) 355/2025); one law-firm note says 1 Aug 2025 (publication date). AGC used. (6) Jurisdiction off Sarawak is before the Federal Court (25-29 Jan 2027); cards state what each law says about its own scope and take no side. (7) Independent verification corrected: Rafizi's '20 to 30 years' is a site-contract term, not a post-closure period; 'books the cut' wording withdrawn for IPCC reporting language; the Southern hub's 5 Mtpa is domestic and regional capacity; neither Federal Court petition concerns carbon storage; Sabah has a carbon-storage licensing provision (Land Ordinance s. 23B).
guardrails_applied: Nothing presented as shipped, signed or operating beyond what is: 'No tonne has shipped', 'unsigned', 'investment decision pending', 'as early as 2031'.
Statute's word 'obligations'/'duties' used, and s. 32(3) fault-liability carve-out stated on fact 2.
Sarawak project not placed under Act 870; hook sub states each law's own scope; no position on the Federal Court dispute.
'Carbon colonialism' and 'dumping ground' not used as FORA's words.
No cost-to-taxpayer figure; levy described only as unset.
Elevated word 'fait accompli' in the view; 'amanah' avoided for its party-name collision.
IPCC rule described as inventory reporting with no credit implied; Japan's own inventory treatment marked unconfirmed; 99% retention and 'generally unresolved' liability on the same card.
Minister's remark carried as 'was reported as saying', with 'then' (he has since left the post), set against the Act's own text.
Southern hub capacity described as Malaysian and regional, not Japanese tonnes.
